 Xgimi is one of several brands that have taken the entry-level and lifestyle projector scene by storm, only to slowly work their way up to increasingly more powerful and sophisticated models.
 When we reviewed the Xgimi Horizon 20 Max earlier this year, we were very impressed indeed, stating that the talented projector was "only a refinement or two away from class-leading greatness".
 But with rivals such as AWOL Vision taking big strides in the last few years – and nabbing this year's What Hi-Fi? Award at this price range – Xgimi has its work cut out for it for the next Horizon series. Have the refinements been enough?
 Latest Videos From What Hi-Fi? 
 Watch full video here: 
 Well, we'll find out very soon. The Xgimi Horizon 30 series is upon us, made up of three models: the Horizon 30 Pro, Horizon 30 Max and Horizon Ultra Max.
 The star of the show, however, is the Xgimi Horizon Ultra Max. The range's top model comes with an incredible claimed brightness of 6,000 lumens and up to 10,000:1 native contrast. That's a five per cent claimed brightness increase over the Horizon 20 Max – and one of the highest lumen figures we've ever seen – and seven times the contrast.

 All three models, however, will now support 4K/120Hz. This is still something of a rarity in the projector world, and twice the refresh rate of the Horizon 20 series.
 The Horizon 30 Pro and Horizon 30 Max models will launch on 1st November, with prices starting at £2099 / $2499. The Horizon 30 Ultra Max releases a tad later on 11th November, priced at £2799 / $3,499.00.

 Several accessories are available too, including stands, ceiling mounts and, yes, 3D glasses.
 The specs certainly sound impressive, but how does this translate to real-life viewing? I got the chance to find out when I saw the new lineup at a launch event in Munich.
 (Image credit: Future) We'll save our final verdict until we get the Horizon 30 series into our test room for comparative testing, of course, but our initial impressions are below.
 What to read next
 I got up close and personal with two competing 4K UST projectors – and I'm more excited than ever for the future of the category

 Adventures In AV: I didn't think I'd ever be excited for 3D again, but this nutty projector prototype changed my mind 
 The Horizon 30 Ultra Max was the model being demonstrated, with clips from several different films shown to us.
 There's no denying that the 30 Ultra Max is bright . During a sunny chase scene through Rome in Fast X, the film shines despite the presence of some ambient light. Several explosions and a flaming, rolling bomb light up the room, and there are some noticeable bright highlights courtesy of the many car headlights.
 Moving on to F1: The Movie and the 30 Ultra Max is terrifically crisp and detailed. We can pick out every line and bit of stubble on Brad Pitt's Sonny Hayes as he prepares to race in the film's opening.
 We were then taken to a room where the Horizon 30 Ultra Max is set up next to its predecessor, the 20 Max. We switch between the two, mid-explosion during a war movie, and the difference in contrast is immediately noticeable, with sparks and flames burning brighter and whiter against an impressively inky sky on the 30 Ultra Max.
 Truth be told, I wasn't able to get a proper listen to the 30 Ultra Max's sound system, which once again features 12W Harman Kardon speakers. Dialogue was at least clear and intelligible despite the hubbub, though what should have been several thrilling action scenes, such as the famous lobby scene from The Matrix , did sound rather tinny.
 We will, of course, give the sound a chance to shine in our dedicated test room, where we'll also have a more in-depth review of the picture quality and compare the projector with market leaders.
 The Horizon 30 series has made several steps in the right direction – it all depends on whether it's enough to keep up with the competition. We'll let you know in our official review.

 In an era dominated by hybrid work and video calls, a dependable webcam is no longer a luxury; it’s an essential upgrade. While modern laptops include built-in cameras, they still struggle with washed-out colors, poor low-light handling, and unflattering angles. A dedicated webcam immediately elevates your setup with sharper image quality, better audio, and flexible positioning that lets you look straight at your audience.
 Today’s standalone cameras have come a long way. Beyond sharper resolutions and reliable autofocus, many now integrate intelligent noise reduction and AI features like auto-framing and subject tracking (such as the Obsbot Tiny SE featured below).
 The right choice comes down to how you plan to use it:

 Streamers and creators will benefit most from 4K resolution and high dynamic range .
 Remote professionals may prefer dependable 1080p video paired with a physical privacy shutter.
 Hybrid commuters will appreciate ultra-compact designs like the Opal Tadpole that easily slip into a travel bag.
 Below, we’ve rounded up the best webcams to help you look sharp and sound clear in every meeting, stream, and call.
 The best webcam overall

 ✅ You want plenty of bang for your buck: The Meet SE offers fantastic image quality and a range of nifty features, all for a very reasonable price.
 ✅ You want to try streaming: The comparatively low entry price of the Meet SE makes it a good choice for anyone looking to dip their toe into the world of streaming.
 Don't buy it if:
 ❌ You want ultra-high-quality video: With a fixed 1080p resolution, the (admittedly very good) picture quality of the Meet SE loses out to rivals offering 4K video.
 ❌ You want something super cheap: While it's still very good value for money, there are more affordable webcams out there if you just need the basics.
 Priced at $69 / £65 / AU$119 and delivering 1080p resolution at up to 100 frames per second, the Obsbot Meet SE offers truly exceptional value for the price - enough to finally unseat the legendary Logitech C920 from its long-standing position as the best webcam overall.
 It significantly outperforms the similarly priced C920 in terms of image quality, features, and overall performance, and its incredibly compact design (with three colors available) looks great too, able to slot unobtrusively into any setup. It also boasts some clever AI-powered features, like effective autofocus and auto-framing, as well as gesture controls - and while the latter might not be for everybody, they're easy to turn off via the bundled Obsbot software.

 ✅ You want full control over your webcam: Thanks to the Insta360 Link Controller software, you are able to tweak the Insta360 Link 2C's settings, apply filters and more for comprehensive control over how you look when using the webcam.
 Don't buy it if:
 ❌ You want 4K at 60fps: The 4K footage the Insta360 Link 2C is capable of looks great, but it's capped at 30fps. For 60fps ultra high definition footage, you'll need something like the Elgato Facecam Pro .
 ❌ You want a budget webcam: With a price tag of $149 / £149 / AU$249, the Insta360 Link 2C won't be making an appearance on our best budget webcams list. Check out the HP 325 FHD Webcam instead.
 The Insta360 Link 2C is currently the best 4K webcam you can buy in 2025. It takes everything we liked about the original Insta360 Link, while adding features and capabilities that make it an excellent webcam upgrade.
 Of course, there's the clear and sharp 4K resolution, but it also comes with new AI-powered tools, such as noise cancellation and tracking which means you'll look (and sound) your very best when using this webcam during video calls.
 Phase Detection Auto Focus is another feature we really loved when reviewing the Insta360 Link 2C, which allows the webcam to intelligently focus on objects that you hold up, making it a great webcam for teachers, tutors and other people who want to show and explain things via video call.
 Unlike a lot of other webcams, the free software for the Insta360 Link 2C, called Insta360 Link Controller, offers a suite of useful settings that with some careful tweaking allows you to get the best possible image quality. Auto-framing uses AI to keep you in shot, and the overall design of the Insta360 Link 2C is stylish and robust. It's not cheap, but this is a quality webcam in almost every sense.

In testing, I found mounting and setup straightforward, whether on a monitor or a tripod, which adds to the Kiyo V2’s appeal for those who need flexibility in their setup.

Luckily, it's more affordable than the Kiyo Pro Ultra it replaces in this guide, despite still delivering plenty of bang for your buck.  Best webcams: FAQs 
 What about those cheap webcams on Amazon or eBay?
 Our list is heavy on big brand names such as HP and Obsbot for good reason. Reputable brands have been tested across many different devices to make sure that the products are compatible with different graphics software. This is why you may see different quality if you use the same camera on a desktop and a laptop - the webcam hardware communicates differently with different devices. 
 Logitech, Obsbot, Razer, and other well-known webcam manufacturers can provide a product that is more likely to work well across a wide range of different machines, so whether you're looking to run your camera on a new gaming desktop or an old Chromebook, you should see similar results. 
 A cheap 1080p/30fps webcam from Amazon or eBay may disappoint you if the drivers and sensors are not up to the same standards as trusted products on our list, so don't take the resolution and framerate as gospel that you'll be getting great video quality. As the saying goes, if it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.
 If you're buying a Logitech webcam, though, you can check out the latest Logitech promo codes for ways to get money off your purchase.
 What should you look for when buying a webcam?
 It's easy to feel a little overwhelmed when looking at webcams to buy – after all, all these cheap models on Amazon look the same, right? Webcams are usually marketed with resolution (720p, 1080p, 4K, etc.) and framerates because this is the most important factor for most people when buying a product, but there are many other considerations that make a webcam 'good' or 'bad'. 
 The first thing to consider is what you need your webcam for. For working professionals or office staff, most conference calling software, such as Zoom or Microsoft Teams, will restrict your broadcast quality to 1080p resolution and 30fps to preserve bandwidth.
 If you're planning on using a webcam purely for these work-related calls, then there's virtually no point in buying a powerful 4K model, as you simply won't see the benefit with most software. The light and color detection will vary for each model, however, so you'll still see a variance in recording quality depending on what webcam you buy. 
 For content creators such as YouTubers or Streamers, there is a range of powerful webcams available, with some reaching 4K resolution and 60fps for buttery smooth video. These webcams are overkill for occasional use, but with features like variable field of view (or FOV) and adjustable resolution and zoom, the extra cost could be a worthy investment in your hobby.
 Can I just use my phone instead of a webcam?
 The quick answer to this is yes! You can indeed ditch your webcam and just use your phone , and that handy link right there will take you to a guide written by our trusted freelancer Alex Blake that explains exactly how to do just that.
 Of course, you'll ideally want a clip mount for your phone if you're planning to replace your webcam like this, so it's not an entirely cost-free method (though a cheap mount won't set you back by much). You'll also require an app to transform your phone into an impromptu webcam, but luckily, the Camo app is completely free .
 The main downside to this method is, of course, that you can't really use your phone while the webcam mode is set up. If you're like me and have regular video meetings but prefer to keep your phone close while working (I get a lot of work-related calls, plus sometimes I've got to keep a comment chain argument going with someone on Reddit - you know how it is), then having your phone clipped to the top of your monitor isn't exactly ideal.
 How to choose the best webcam for you 
 As the world returns to something resembling normalcy, the best webcams for laptops and PCs are finally back in stock. Whether they’re from Microsoft , Razer, Logitech , or one of the cheaper brands whose products punch above their weight, there’s a plethora of choices to pick from to help you upgrade your streaming or video conferencing.
 Since more communication is happening online these days, it’s crucial to have your Zoom calls with friends and video conferencing meetings that are crystal clear. And, that means you need to invest in one of the best webcams for your computer setup. It’s true that most laptops or all-in-one computers already come with a webcam installed but having a dedicated one will offer more features and higher resolutions.
 It doesn’t matter if you’re trying to keep in touch with your extended network, putting together the perfect work-from-home setup, or getting ready for back-to-school season, invest in one of these made-for-computer cameras to make sure your family and colleagues can see your bright, shiny face. From the webcams ideal for game streaming to excellent webcams for Zoom , we’ve collected our top picks here as well as included our price comparison tool to help you find the best deal .
 How we test the best webcams 
 Here at TechRadar, we don't use any specific testing programs to benchmark a webcam as their quality differences should be visually noticeable. Instead, models will be stacked up against products with similar specifications and prices to see how they compare, as well as running through a few real-world testing scenarios.
 We keep lighting levels consistent and test for well-lit and low-light conditions to put the webcam sensor through its paces. Webcams with unsatisfactory sensors struggle if a subject isn't well-lit, resulting in a fuzzy 'static' like interference known as background noise. We make note of how accurate the colors are in any recorded footage and the overall clarity of video and photographs taken on the webcam.
 We also compare features like field-of-view (often abbreviated to FOV), frame rate, and resolution, as well as any supporting software that ships with the product. Operating systems like Windows 11 have a camera application capable of making minimal adjustments to contrast and hue, but there are branded applications like Razer Synapse and Logi Tune that can better adjust your footage.
 The hardware itself will also be checked for mounting options and available movements, such as a swivel ball joint or fixed positioning. Finally, any onboard microphone will be checked for clarity and its ability to filter out background noise, though it's worth mentioning that most webcams on the market have quite poor-quality microphones when compared to the best headsets or the best USB mics .

 Professional cameras are cool. Do you know what they're not? Fun. The best instant cameras, though? Now they're fun — a way to take a snap and get an instant snapshot of a moment, forever frozen on a small piece of photo paper. Perfect for events, for parties, for vacations; an instant camera is a great way to disconnect from the digital world and remember what it's like to be a real human.
 We've put loads of different instant cameras so that we can find the best around, thoroughly checking all their features and how well they take those snaps. If you're looking for a new camera, we know all the best options.
 The best right now is the Fujifilm Instax mini Evo . It's a slightly more expensive option, but its image quality is the very best we've ever seen, and its compact form factor fits into a bag with no issues at all. A bit too rich for your blood? No problem, there are cameras here to suit every budget. Here are the best instant cameras of 2026.

 Why you can trust Tom's Guide 
 While they may not be professional devices, we still put the best instant cameras through their paces to find out which one you should buy. That's thanks to our dedicated camera testing team, who love taking photos with cameras big and small. Most of the reviews you'll find here are taken by keen photographer Nikita Achant a, who, before writing for Tom's Guide, was a sub-editor and writer for Canon EMEA. Then there's Reviews Senior Editor Peter Wolinski , who takes professional shots alongside running Tom's Guide's reviews team.
 Here are the tests the reviews team put the best instant cameras through before they land on the list proper.
 We take them out and shoot some pictures. What better way is there to see how well a camera works than to take some pictures and compare them to its closest competitor? Not many, that's for sure.
 We try different lighting. Just because a camera works well in daylight doesn't mean it's going to work well when things get darker. We make sure to take photos in a bunch of different conditions to get a better idea of performance in different lighting scenes.
 Making sure it's easy to use. A point-and-shoot camera can't get you bogged down in image settings and other options. You should be able to point it at a thing, press the shutter, and get an image spat out with a whir. Anything more would be too complicated.
 Is there an app and is it good. We install any companion apps and test them — they're something that can get in the way of taking snaps as much as they can help, so we want to make sure that they work well.

 What to look for when buying an instant camera 
 Instant cameras are not exactly instant. You have to wait at least 90 seconds for the picture to "fill in" to view the finished result, but we often found it took several minutes for the completed image to fully bake, revealing richer color and sharper focus.
 Zink vs. Fujifilm Instax 
 Some instant cameras use the Fujifilm Instax film cartridges, which come in several sizes and varieties. This is the photo paper that Polaroid cameras have traditionally used: the paper is exposed to light, and the chemicals react to produce an image.
 Other instant cameras use Zink paper, which uses heat to activate colors in the paper. The advantage to Zink is that you don’t have to worry about accidentally exposing the paper to light, as you do with Instax film. However, we’ve found that Zink prints tended to be less vibrant overall.
 Does it print everything you shoot? 
 With traditional instant cameras, every photo you took was printed out. That's still the case for a good number of modern instant cameras, but given the cost of film, that approach can be very pricey — 50 cents and higher per shot, in some cases. However, some instant cameras now let you preview each shot so you can decide if you want to print it out or not. It could save you money in the long run.
 Digital storage 
 While not universal, some of the new instant cameras have a microSD card slot, and save a digital copy of every photo you take. Not only does this make it easier to make a second print, but you can also share that photo on social media a lot more easily.
 Smartphone app 
 Still other instant cameras can connect via Bluetooth to a smartphone app. This opens up a few more features, such as the ability to use the camera to print photos taken with your smartphone, add filters, stickers, and more.
 FAQs 
 Here are the answers to some of the frequently asked questions about instant cameras.
 Do people still use instant cameras?
 Of course! Just look at all the options on the list here available for purchase. They're a wonderful way to get reconnected with the photos that you take. They're easy to use and loads of fun. They might be a blast from the past, but they're more than here to stay for long haul.
 What's better, an instant camera or digital camera?
 That really depends on use case. If you're after the sharpest, professional-looking photos and the flexibility to do serious photo editing, then one of the best mirrorless cameras is what you need. However, if you want something casual, fun and easy to use, that produces instant stylized prints, there's nothing better than an instant camera. If you're primarily taking photos of friends at social events, and/or you want to share prints, an instant cameras are the best (and most affordable) choice.
 Which is better, Instax Wide, Square or mini?
 None are necessarily better. However, you should consider which you want before you buy your Instax instant camera, as each camera can only use a set film. Instax mini is better for quicker prints, sharing and scrapbooking, as it's smaller. Instax Wide is better for things like travel and documentary photography, wider scenes with friends and landscapes, thanks to its sweeping field of view. Instax Square is the middle ground, so is a versatile all rounder. Price also scales upwards from mini to Wide, so make sure to factor that into your choice.
 Is Instax owned by Polaroid?
 No. Instax is owned by Fujifilm, while Polaroid is a separate company. Many people use the word "Polaroid" as a synonym for instant camera, which is a misnomer.
 Each brand creates its own film and camera. Polaroid film has that classic retro instant camera styling, although Fujifilm is legendary for its film and color science, so also produces very retro-styled film. 
 Other instant camera manufacturers include Kodak and Lomography.
 Do instant photos last forever?
 Just like any printed photo medium, instant photos do not last forever. They can get bleached by the sun, and they detoriate over time. They're a fleeting thing, although you can lengthen their lives with frames and by keeping them out of direct sunlight. Or just pop it in your wallet.
 Are instant cameras suitable for children?
 Depends on the age of the child. There aren't any horrible chemicals to worry about, and the devices themselves tend to be super sturdy, but that won't stop small fingers potentially ruining the prints as they come out of the camera. Still, there's nothing easier than an instant camera when it comes to taking snaps!
 We'd say that a child over 8-9 wouldn't struggle with an instant camera — although you'll want to watch how many snaps they're taking. The print cartridges are not cheap. A small digital camera might be a better bet to avoid trigger-happy snapping and costly cartridge bills.
 How we test instant cameras 
 We test instant cameras in the same way we test full mirrorless cameras: that is to say, we put them through their paces. Obviously, we look at how much the camera costs, but we also consider how much money you're going to spend in the long term, too, with things like film cost, ink cartridge prices and battery expenditure.
 Then we test the cameras in a range of scenarios to give a complete evaluation of their pros and cons. We'll always test out our instant cameras shooting in the types of places and scenarios you would: indoor selfies with friends, group shots, outdoors in the street and, of course, with any cute pets we come across along the way!
 We always make sure to shoot with the cameras in daylight as well as low light to work out how well the cameras perform in challenging conditions. We test out all of their features and components to see how much control they will give you over exposure and how much creativity they'll offer with things like filters.
 (Image credit: Future) This naturally allows us to test out the camera's focusing and any other neat features, like screens, audio recording or digital storage. After all this, we'll have a great feel (literally) of what the camera feels like in use, how comfortable it is to hold, and how well its built.
 If there's an app, we'll use it to edit our photos, as well as print smartphone images if we can. Of course, we print out all our instant photos and evaluate the quality of the prints, the aesthetic of the camera filters and film, plus the colors, sharpness and definition. While doing this, we also get a good idea of how long the camera spends printing.
 What does all this mean? That you can rest assured we've put the instant cameras in this list through rigorous testing, and the best picks come highly recommended.

 Once you have been in the home cinema game for a while, it can be easy to forget about what brought you there in the first place.
 Although it is one of the most dedicated groups of fans that you can come across, you can find yourself forgetting the initial sense of wonder that came with hearing an incredible sound system or seeing a film with a projector outside of the cinema for the first time.
 I remember watching Arcane on the Award-winning Sony Bravia Projector 8 (which launched at a staggering £15,999 / $15999 / AU$21999) back in 2024 when I joined the What Hi-Fi? team, and being absolutely awestruck by the level of detail and contrast that the premium projector offers.
 Latest Videos From What Hi-Fi? 
 Watch full video here: 
 While other systems can still give me that feeling of wonder, it is not as frequent as when I first started the job.
 But this old husk was reminded of the brilliance of home cinema when I attended a grassroots cinema club last week. Run by movie fan Will Mead, Midweek Cinema hosts movie screenings in various pubs across London primarily at the start of the week.
 You may like

 “Good sound is good sound, regardless of whether it's hi-fi or home cinema” – how a surprise product reminded me of this simple truth

 The club has also just been given access to the newly reopened Plaza Camden, which was thought to have closed its doors as a cinema back in February. But the venue is being given a new lease of life, and Midweek Cinema now operates from a 72-seater cinema screen for some of the week.
 Don't worry, the projector (Image credit: Future) I got the chance to attend one of the screenings, kicking off with A Panic at Needle Park . I’ll be the first to admit that it was not a film that I had heard of, but I quickly learnt that it stars Al Pacino in his first major role. The movie follows Bobby (Pacino) and Helen (Kitty Winn), who fall in love, but their addiction to heroin forces them go to any means necessary to get high.

 Tucked away in the ground floor of a cosy pub in West London, the small but passionate audience was treated to a bowl of popcorn each before the film began. Everyone is encouraged to talk to each other if they would like before and after the film as well, and plenty of regulars turned up.
 Will’s setup includes the Hisense C2 Ultra projector, a pop-up foldable screen and a portable PA system for the audio. Now, that's not the reference-style system we'd expect to see in our home cinema room; there's no AVR or surround sound system involved, and (understandably) 4K discs aren't always the priority.
 But that didn't matter quite as much here, as the system serves as a way for people to connect and enjoy films together, and ultimately that's what I think home cinema should be all about.
 What to read next
 The What Hi-Fi? readers have spoken and the age of streaming is not a golden one for home cinema – all hail the Blu-ray 
 “When the DVD format arrived, “Home Cinema” really took off, helped by the rapid development of TVs” – veteran AV experts discuss the biggest shifts in TV and home cinema during What Hi-Fi?'s 50-year lifetime 
 Are giant TVs a threat to projectors? We asked the industry to find out 
 In fact, the four-star Hisense C2 Ultra's middling black levels and somewhat flat colours didn't distract, or even really cross my mind. The versatility, easy set-up and punchy high brightness that this projector boasts were perfect for this situation, making it an ideal choice for Will.
 As the lights went off and the crowd settled, the magic of seeing a film with others was all that mattered. Sure, it wasn’t on a premium projector, and the sound wasn't coming from a £10,000 system, but sharing a movie with a group was really touching.
 No gatekeeping, no competitive specs comparison; just watching a film with fellow movie nerds. I’ll certainly be testing my next projector and sound system with a renewed passion.

 The audio quality with the DJI Mic Mini 2S is great, and the environmental noise cancellation makes it easy to use. You don’t need to worry about any unwanted background noise. The battery life is more than enough for day-to-day use, and the price is very attractive compared to other mics in the DJI range, such as the DJI Mic 3, which costs £259.
 32-bit float audio
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) With 32-bit float audio capture, the DJI Mic Mini 2S can record a huge dynamic range — more than the human ear can hear. So, if there are quieter parts of the recording that are important, it's very easy to boost these in post-production. It also means that screeching sounds, like screams, for example, won't be clipped, and instead can simply be made quieter in post.
 This is a feature of the DJI Mic 3, but not the earlier Mic Mini models, so having a flagship feature on a cheaper product like the 2S is nothing to be sniffed at.
 The mics have 14.5GB of internal storage, which means they can hold around 22 hours of 32-bit float audio, or 28 hours of 24-bit float audio recording.

 Audio quality: Fricatives/sibilance
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The microphone records sound, and especially airy sounds known as fricatives and sibilance, very well. These include sounds such as ‘s’, ‘sh’ and ‘f’. Sounds like this tend to cause whistling in the microphone, which is harsh for listeners, but that wasn’t an issue with this microphone.
 As you can hear in the audio recording above, the words are clear without any distortion. However, plosives are a different story, and I’ll discuss that later on.
 Simple connectivity
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Connectivity with the DJI Mic Mini 2S couldn't be easier. The most straightforward way to use the plug-in USB-C receiver, but if you have a DJI camera you open the door to the DJI OsmoAudio Ecosystem.
 When using the mic as part of the ecosystem, you can connect to any DJI devices without needing the receiver. You can also connect to traditional cameras using a 3.5mm cable, USB-C or simply via Blueutooth.
 The transmitters and receiver of the DJI Mic Mini 2S have backward compatibility with older models, too. These include the Mic Mini and Mic Mini 2 transmitters, and you can connect up to four. You can mix and match, allowing you to upgrade your older setup with the latest noise-cancelling capabilities and 32-bit float rate by simply buying a Mic Mini 2S transmitter.
 Environmental noise cancellation
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) When I made the recording you can listen to above, I had my work laptop in front of me. As any remote worker will know, it tends to pop and ping with notifications almost eternally, and it was no different when I was delicately performing my tongue twisters.
 I had to stop to re-record the clip a few times because of the notifications, but I finally decided to just keep going, and to my surprise, there wasn’t a single notification sound on the finished recording. The DJI Mic Mini 2S microphones use two-level noise-cancelling technology, which identifies and reduces unwanted background noise. The standard Mic Mini 2 struggles a little here, making the audio sound underwater, so the 2S is certainly an upgrade.
 Battery life
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Each DJI Mic Mini 2S transmitter has 11 hours of battery life, which is more than the eight hours of the DJI Mic 3 . The receiver of the Mic Mini 2S holds 10 hours of battery and the charging case gives a total of 40 hours of runtime.
 This is more than enough battery for my usage, which is talking to a camera three times a week, and recording voice-overs for my videos. And for amateur creators taking the microphone out on a weekend-long adventure, it has enough power to carry you through most recording stints without reaching for a power pack.
 Price
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) The DJI Mic Mini 2S is available for purchase in the U.K. for £169 from Amazon or the DJI online store. This is the version I tested, with two transmitters, but you can also get a cheaper version with one transmitter for £79 .
 Unfortunately, you cannot purchase the Mic Mini 2S in the U.S. just yet due to ongoing regulatory and import restrictions against DJI, but you can still buy the older DJI Mic Mini for $99 at Amazon U.S. 
 Depending on what you need the mic for, you could opt to get the DJI Mic Mini 2, but this only connects two mics to the receiver, whereas the 2S can connect four.
 If you want the flagship DJI Mic 3, you’re going to be paying £259. Going for a cheaper option and getting similar battery life, the same core mic components, and a similar level of environmental noise performance is — to me — a no-brainer.
 DJI Mic Mini 2S review: What I don’t like 
 Plosive sounds
 Bulky receiver
 Although this is one of the best microphones for content creation, it comes with two minor flaws. The letter ‘p’ is picked up very strongly by the microphone, and the receiver is a bit too bulky.
 Audio quality (Plosives)
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) Although the audio is generally very impressive, when it comes to plosives, the microphone seems to struggle. These are notoriously difficult sounds, including the likes of ‘p’, ‘b’, ‘d’ and ‘g’. The most noticeable issue was with the ‘p’ sounds at the start of words, which sounded very harsh. I could hear the air pushing into the microphone.
 This makes listening quite tiresome, as the pinching and popping sounds will put people off listening to the audio. This issue isn’t present in the DJI Mic Mini 2. It’s worth noting that these sounds can also be due to microphone etiquette (how close you hold the microphone to your mouth), so your performance will be better or worse depending on how you use the microphone.
 Receiver design is bulky
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) This isn’t the end of the world, but the plug-in receiver for the DJI Mic Mini 2S is quite bulky. Depending on what it’s plugged into, it can make your device top-heavy or sit awkwardly on the table. When plugged into my phone, I can’t stand the phone up or lay it flat, which makes it feel a little cumbersome.
 For ease of use, the Insta360 Mic Air is a better choice because it’s less bulky. This makes it more comfortable for longer recording sessions.
 DJI Mic Mini 2S review: How does it compare? 
 So, how does the DJI Mic Mini 2S measure up against its competitors? It certainly holds its own, and although it costs more than the budget Insta360 Mic Air (£69), I think it’s worth the extra spend. The DJI Mic Mini 2 (£89) is a lot cheaper than the 2S, but it’s still worth the extra spend if you’re planning to record in noisy environments and want to keep ambient sound out of your audio. The additional AI noise cancellation technology is what steps up this microphone, as it makes editing audio in post-production far easier.
 (Image credit: Tom's Guide) I think the DJI Mic Mini 2S is the perfect option for anyone who wants to up their content game but is new to wireless microphones. Another good option is the Rode Wireless Micro for £139, as these clip-on microphones are also good for filtering ‘pop’ sounds, but for professional video makers, the DJI is still the best choice for quality.
 DJI Mic Mini 2S review: Who should buy it? 
 The DJI Mic Mini 2S microphone has great audio quality. The environmental noise cancellation technology silenced all outside noise in my recordings, and it isolated my voice so it was crystal clear. The microphones also have a long battery life, and with the charging case you can get up to 40 hours of use. I think this microphone is great value for money as you get all of the perks of the flagship DJI models at a fraction of the price.
 Though I love the microphones, there are obvious popping sounds when pronouncing plosives. The receiver is also bulky, so you’ll need to keep this in mind depending on the device you’re transmitting to.
 I recommend the DJI Mic Mini 2S for content creators who need to level up their audio, especially if a lot of their work is done outside with lots of ambient sound.

It does everything the best portable projectors need to do - consistently serving up what we describe as "scintillating visuals", whether we were streaming TV and movies or playing games.
 We loved pretty much everything about the C2 Ultra - from the high build quality (including the remote, which is rare) to the superb picture and audio quality. The OS felt snappy in use, and gave us access to all the core apps we expect.
 Now, the size and weight do make this a genuinely portable unit. However, it's worth noting that it does need constant mains power, which means you won't be able to use it on-the-go in the same way you'd use a projector like the Anker Nebula Mars 3. For most people looking for a smart projector to take room to room, that's won't be a deal-breaker.

 We were already big fans of the original Samsung the Freestyle mini projector, naming it our top choice. And it's stayed that way - until we tried out the second-generation model.
 Samsung's The Freestyle 2nd Generation isn't a radical departure from the previous iteration - although it now includes a Gaming Hub, letting you connect a wireless controller and access cloud-basing gaming apps like Xbox and Nvidia GeForce Now. It's all very easy to set-up, which is a big part of The Freestyle's appeal, and the subtle, compact design makes it ideal for transporting in a backpack.
 In use, picture quality is good - blacks are deep and colors are accurate, with HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG support. The projector also features what Samsung dubs '360 Degree' sound. And in our tests, we were surprised to find it really did offer spacious audio, although the bass was admittedly limited.
 However, we did spot a few drawbacks. In our multiple luminance tests, this wasn't the brightest portable projector in the world, and the contrast is low, too, for daytime use outdoors. We would've liked to see more than a single micro-HDMI port here, too (or at least include a HDMI adapter in the box). It may not be a budget model, either, but overall, this is an excellent, easy-to-use mini projector with a real emphasis on portability.

 The BenQ GP520 is an affordable 4K portable projector that boasts impressive brightness - the LED light source hits around 2,600 ANSI Lumens, and in our review, we called it “a go-anywhere all-in-one theater system.”
 The design is boxy and compact, weighing in at 8.2lb / 3.7kg. There’s no built-in handle - although you can get a carry case (sold separately). Despite this, we found it easy enough and light enough to move around. There’s no gimbal stand, but you’ll also find tripod holds on three sides for positioning the projector.
 Picture quality is very good. We found the 4K images were sharp and detailed with HDR10+ support, and there’s motion handling. Colors aren’t blisteringly vivid, though, and the blacks could be deeper. This isn’t one for gamers either, since it can’t switch to 1080p for a frame-rate boost. Having said that, under the right settings, it looks way better than it has any right to be for a low-cost 4K portable projector. We also felt the speakers were surprisingly good. Of course, you’ll get better performance with a sound system, but they’re absolutely acceptable without an external set-up - especially since the fans aren’t especially loud in use.
 Overall, a solid 4K entry that’s hard to beat on price, especially given the higher than average brightness compared to similar models.

 Best portable projectors: FAQs 
 Do more lumens mean a better projector?
 We asked Bob Wudeck, Senior Director, Business Development, at BenQ
 Lumens for projectors is like horsepower in a car – it’s important but only a part of how well the projector is suited for the task. In the past lumens were the most important element. Now things are different, as most projectors today are far more advanced than projectors sold five years ago. So – what makes for a better projector?
 Color accuracy – While commercial cinema projectors have strict color standards, there are still many classroom and conference room projectors that are not very color accurate. For newer home theater and commercial projectors, Rec. 709 is the standard for color accuracy and measurement to look for in the specifications.
 Resolution – While nearly every TV sold today has over 8 million pixels, you can still buy a projector with under 1 million pixels today. The bigger the screen, the more pixels needed for a nicely detailed image. Look for either 1080p or 4K UHD native resolution projectors for the highest pixel density.
 Solid State Lighting – Projector lamps contain mercury, are expensive, and need to be replaced every few years. They are being replaced by solid state light sources like lasers and high brightness LEDs that last up to 30,000 hours. Today you can get a high brightness LED projector with 4,000 lumens and higher color accuracy for only a small premium over a similar lamp powered projector.
 Throw Ratio – Depending on your setup, the right throw ratio will make a big difference. For example, if you are using a golf simulator, you will want a “short throw” projector that can be mounted in a location that enables you to play without casting a shadow on the screen. Use a projector calculator to see how far back your model needs to be mounted to fill your screen.
 What's the difference between ISO and ANSI?
 A lumen is a measurement of brightness, and when it comes to portable projectors, that's important, especially if you're viewing a screen during the day or in an environment that's not completely dark like a cinema. 
 When selecting the right model, you'll likely come across both ISO and ANSI ratings. The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and American National Standards Institute (ANSI) are two different organizations measuring brightness. ANSI lumens measure the total light output, while ISO simulates a more real-world environment using a black-and-white checkerboard display. Because of this, they're not directly comparable. 1 ISO lumen converts to around 1.25 ANSI lumens.
 While higher numbers should mean brighter images either way, it doesn't necessarily mean it'll be better than others. It'll depend on the settings and the portable projector's own capabilities. 
 Can I watch Netflix on my mini projector?
 We asked Bob Wudeck, Senior Director, Business Development, at BenQ
 For a portable projector, it should be easy to have Netflix running on your phone and then pair your phone with the projector so that you get Netflix (or other streaming apps) shown in the big screen format afforded by the projector. However, many paid streaming apps like Netflix, Prime Video, Hulu, and Disney Plus have copy protection that prevents mirroring from mobile devices due to policies enacted and enforced by content owners. So, if you are casting from a notebook, Netflix content can be cast wirelessly via your laptop’s Google Chrome browser that is connected to an HDMI cable. You can also use Chromecast or Apple TV wireless devices to stream content as well. The best models of mini projectors also have phone apps to enable you to control your streams right from your phone or device to make it easy to use.
 Can you connect a phone to a projector?
 We asked Bob Wudeck, Senior Director, Business Development, at BenQ
 There are three easy ways to connect a phone to a projector:
 Cable – Nearly every iPhone and Android device has a video output port. Most projectors still use HDMI as their standard input port, so a simple adapter from either the USB-C connector on an Android or HDMI connector on the iPhone will enable you to get the cable connected – all you need to do is change the source to start screen mirroring from your phone to a projector.
 Casting – If you have a Chromecast or an Apple TV, you can wirelessly connect to your projector and mirror your screen. You will need to be on the same network as the receiver, then use your built-in screen mirroring to send it to your projector. This is a nice option when you want to show photos or videos on your device, or for occasional use.
 Wireless Presentation System – For business or education use, a wireless presentation system is faster and more secure than the other two options. The best models enable you to plug in a button to your phone or tablet and start sharing instantly. Others use either a dedicated app installed on your phone or Airplay to share the screen. While they are more expensive, the best models encrypt the transmission, so sensitive information can’t be wirelessly captured and seen from curious people in the area.
 Are portable projectors any good?
 Yes! Think of it like the difference between a portable Bluetooth speaker and the speakers in your living room. The latter may sound better and go louder, but you can't exactly pop them in a bag and take them to the beach. Even taking them into the garden is an enormous pain.
 It's the same with portable projectors. They're typically – but not always – less bright and less powerful than their wired siblings, but they compensate for that by being incredibly practical with go-anywhere abilities. Battery-powered portable projectors are more than capable of delivering movie night without you having to worry about finding a power socket, and their portability means they're easy to move around and very simple and quick to set up.
 That doesn't mean they're just for the great outdoors, though. Because portable projectors are designed to be small, they're useful for rooms where you don't want or can't have a normal-sized projector, or for homes where you might not want the projector in the same room all of the time.
 The main compromise with portable projectors is in brightness: that's the biggest drain on their power, so battery-powered projectors have to strike a balance between the brightness of the picture (which in turn affects the maximum range and size of their display) and the amount of time they can run for between recharges. 
 What's the difference between a projector and a mini projector?
 The main difference between a standard projector and a mini projector is that traditional projectors are designed to produce the highest possible quality at the most significant possible size, and if that means more giant bulbs or LED assemblies and louder fans, then so be it. Mini projectors also deliver good quality, but their priorities are different: they're also designed with portability and price in mind, so they're often more portable and affordable than their bigger siblings and often include built-in speakers and easy Bluetooth speaker connectivity.
 Standard projectors are mainly powered, but many mini projectors are also designed to run on battery power. Like any battery-powered device, they have limited running times compared to when they're plugged in, but most models have more than enough power to show multiple movies without requiring a recharge halfway through. It can also mean that the projector is dimmer than a wired one to get more life out of the battery.
 The other key difference is that mini projectors are designed to be set up speedily, and that can mean they have fewer connection options than wired models. However, the growing adoption of wireless technologies such as Google Cast and AirPlay and intelligent TV-style features such as streaming apps that work over Wi-Fi means that many mini projectors can get video from many sources.
 How to choose the best portable projector for you 
 It’s important to know what to look for when you're buying a portable projector.
 By considering how you’re going to use it, you’ll get the right mix of features. We asked Luke Chen, senior business line manager at Viewsonic Europe, a display and projector specialist for his point of view (no pun intended).
 First off, you need to think about the situations you’re going to be using your projector in and find one that fits your requirements. Taking your smart projector on-the-go? Consider how well the projector achieves a portable design. Does it come with a carry handle? Or can it fold into a travel-ready container? If your projector is going to sit on your coffee table, make sure it says it’s a “short throw.”
 Think about durability, LED technology avoids dimming projector issues, allowing smart projectors to shine brightly for up to 30,000 hours. LED light sources run much cooler than bulb-based light sources (meaning less fan noise). “Lamp-Free” is what to look for. It means you no longer have to rely on bulbs, which need to be replaced over time. They’re eco-friendly, too. Lamp Free means no glass bulb is needed, which means no mercury.
 Something else to consider is resolution. Smart projectors are much smaller than standard projectors, this makes resolution the first thing to go. For those who enjoy camping, and just want some form of entertainment next to the campfire, a lower resolution works. Mini projectors have the hardest time with resolution. But, not all smart projectors suffer from poor resolution. 4K Smart LED projectors are now on the market. If home entertainment is your preferred use, opt for 4K resolution. The highest-end smart projectors will call themselves “True 4K” projectors.
 Next, up, apps. Your projector is only as smart as the apps running on it. So, it makes sense to have an app store enabled on your projector. Does the projector you’re looking at come with app store integration? To work with apps, enable voice commands, and stream movies (all at the same time) look for a smart projector with ample processors, memory, and storage.
 Most smart projectors have to compromise on sound. This is the only way to fit all the components into such a small size. If you don’t already have a premium sound system integrated into your home theatre, opt for premium speakers. In short, there’s no such thing as a one-size-fits-all projector.
 How we test the best portable projectors 
 We've tested many different types of projectors over the years, including the best ultra-short throw projectors and the best business projectors - but when we were looking for the best portable projector, we needed to see a few key considerations.
 The most obvious is portability. This means different things to different people. In the guide above, we've clarified that some designs are portable because you can move them from room to room, like the Anker Nebula Cosmos Laser 4K. At the same time, others are pocket-sized, like the ASUS ZenBeam E1 Portable LED Projector. Both are, technically, 'portable' but to varying degrees, and we've made that clear in the guide.
 Usability is critical with projectors. There's no point carrying one with you if setting up is a pain. So while testing these best portable projectors, we ensured that you could get up and running quickly, even if you've not had much experience with projectors.
 Brightness and picture quality vary in our guide above, but all can project TV shows and movies at a decent rate. We were mainly looking for projectors that offered a decent amount of brightness and resolution for their size and value for money. We've clarified when you'll likely get a dimmer experience, but in a tiny and affordable package, which might be more of a priority for some people.

 Native streaming: the projector runs its own licensed apps, so the iPhone is optional after setup.

 DRM and HDCP: The Streaming Reality Check You Need to Know
 Before we get into the individual reviews, let me save you the most common frustration we saw in testing. If you plan to mirror Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime Video, or Hulu from your iPhone or Android to a mini projector, you’ll likely hit an HDCP wall.
 HDCP (High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection) is copy protection built into streaming apps. When you try to mirror these apps via standard AirPlay or Miracast, most projectors – including every wireless model under $100 – will display a black screen or an “HDCP unauthorized” error. It’s not a bug; it’s a deliberate licensing restriction.
 Three real workarounds we tested that actually work:
 Use a TV Stick: Plug a Fire TV Stick, Roku Streaming Stick, or Chromecast directly into the projector’s HDMI port. The stick handles DRM natively and streams Netflix/Disney+ at full quality without mirroring.
 Choose a projector with officially licensed Netflix: The WEMI X7 and Wielio 2026 both ship with Android TV/Google Play access, letting you install Netflix directly on the projector (no phone mirroring required).
 Use screen mirroring only for non-DRM content: YouTube, TikTok, personal videos, presentations, and Apple TV+ mirror without issues in our testing.
 This is the single biggest buying decision factor most reviews skip. If you mainly want Netflix/streaming, prioritize a projector with built-in Android TV. If you mainly want YouTube and personal media, any wireless projector will work fine.
 How to Connect Your Phone to a Mini Projector
 Connection method depends entirely on your phone. Here’s what actually works based on our hands-on testing.
 Connecting an iPhone to a Mini Projector
 Option 1: Wireless via AirPlay (no adapter needed). Make sure the projector and iPhone are on the same Wi-Fi network. Open Control Center on your iPhone, tap Screen Mirroring, and select the projector from the list. Works flawlessly on the YGSKK, WEMI X7, and Wielio 2026 in our testing.
 Option 2: Wired via Lightning to HDMI adapter. Plug Apple’s official Lightning Digital AV Adapter ($49) into your iPhone, then run an HDMI cable to the projector’s HDMI port. This bypasses HDCP issues for some apps but adds cable clutter.
 One-step iPhone options: If you want to skip the AirPlay menu dance, the YGSKK and LYNCAST X1 both auto-detect iPhones via their built-in mirroring apps – no menu diving required.
 Connecting an Android Phone to a Mini Projector
 Option 1: Wireless via Miracast (Samsung, Xiaomi, OnePlus, etc.). Swipe down to Quick Settings, tap Cast/Smart View/Screen Mirroring, and select your projector. Works on 90% of Android phones we’ve tested.
 Option 2: Wireless via manufacturer apps. Many projectors (YGSKK, Magcubic, AKIYO) ship with their own casting apps – usually named “CastPlay,” “Smart Cast,” or similar. These often have fewer HDCP restrictions than native Miracast.
 Option 3: P2P Direct (no WiFi needed). The AKIYO O1 supports peer-to-peer direct casting – your phone creates a direct link to the projector without needing a Wi-Fi network. Perfect for camping or hotel rooms with bad WiFi.
 Option 4: USB-C to HDMI cable. Most modern Android phones (USB-C port) support direct HDMI output via a $10 USB-C to HDMI cable. This is the most reliable method for HDCP-protected content.
 Common Android issue we saw: Some Samsung phones aggressively kill background casting apps after 5-10 minutes, especially in battery-saver mode. Disable battery optimization for the casting app if you experience dropouts.
 Wired vs Wireless: Which Is Better?
 Wired connections are more reliable and bypass most HDCP issues, but require you to buy an adapter ($10-$49) and deal with a cable. Wireless connections are cleaner but can lag, drop, or hit HDCP walls. For casual YouTube viewing, wireless is fine. For Netflix marathons or gaming, go wired.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Right Mini Projector for Phones?
 After testing 12 projectors, here’s what actually matters when choosing the best mini projector for your phone.
 Brightness and ANSI Lumens: Marketing vs Reality
 Every mini projector claims 5,000 to 15,000 lumens. None of them are accurate. “Lumens” without the ANSI prefix are usually marketing fiction measured under ideal lab conditions.
 ANSI lumens are the industry standard. We verified our picks against an independent light meter:
 Under 100 ANSI: KODAK Luma 150, AKASO WT50, AKASO Cookie. Requires near-total darkness.
 100-300 ANSI: YGSKK, LYNCAST X1, Wielio, Magcubic, AKIYO, ClokoWe. Works in dim rooms, struggles with ambient light.
 300+ ANSI: WEMI X7 (2000 ANSI). Handles moderate daylight.
 Rule of thumb: for dark bedrooms, 100 ANSI is enough. For living rooms with curtains, you want 300+. For outdoor dusk viewing, 500+ is ideal. For daylight viewing, only the WEMI X7 in this list qualifies.
 Native vs Supported Resolution
 “1080P supported” and “native 1080P” are not the same thing. A 720P native projector can accept a 1080P signal but displays it at 720P. The image looks softer than true 1080P, especially at 80+ inches.
 Native 1080P projectors in our test: WEMI X7, YGSKK, Wielio, AKASO WT50, CiBest W13, KODAK Luma 150 (input).
 For movie watching, 720P native is acceptable at 80-100 inches. For spreadsheets, presentations, or text-heavy content, native 1080P matters more.
 Wireless Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6 vs 5G WiFi vs Miracast
 Wi-Fi 6 is the newest standard – faster, more stable, and handles 4K content without buffering. Available on: WEMI X7, YGSKK, Maypug, LYNCAST X1, Wielio, Magcubic.
 5G WiFi is the previous standard – fast enough for 1080P streaming but can struggle with 4K. Available on: AKIYO, ClokoWe.
 Miracast and AirPlay are wireless protocols for screen mirroring. AirPlay works only for Apple devices; Miracast works for most Android phones.
 P2P Direct (AKIYO O1) is unique – it creates a direct wireless link between your phone and projector without needing a Wi-Fi network. Best for travel and off-grid use.
 Smart Features and Built-In Apps
 Projectors with built-in Android TV or Google Play (WEMI X7, Wielio, LYNCAST X1) let you install Netflix, Prime Video, YouTube, and Disney+ directly on the projector – bypassing your phone entirely. This eliminates most HDCP headaches.
 Projectors without built-in apps (CiBest, KODAK Luma, AKASO models) require screen mirroring from your phone or an external streaming stick.
 Battery vs Plug-In
 Battery-powered models (KODAK Luma 150, AKASO WT50, AKASO Cookie) offer true portability but limit you to 2-2.5 hours and dimmer images due to battery size constraints.
 Plug-in models (everything else) deliver brighter images and unlimited runtime but require an outlet. For backyard movie nights, plug-in is usually better – just run an extension cord.
 Price Tiers and Value
 Ultra-Budget (under $50): CiBest W13, AKIYO O1, Maypug P3, LYNCAST X1. Best for casual bedroom and dorm use.
 Budget ($50-100): ClokoWe HY300, YGSKK, Magcubic. Best value sweet spot.
 Mid-Range ($100-200): Wielio 2026, WEMI X7. Best for living rooms and frequent use.
 Premium ($200+): KODAK Luma 150, AKASO WT50, AKASO Cookie. Best for travel and battery-powered use.
 What Makes a Projector “Mini”
 True mini projectors weigh under 2 lbs and fit in a backpack. We tested models ranging from 209g (AKASO Cookie) to 1.8 kg (WEMI X7). Anything over 3 lbs stops being portable – that’s a “portable” projector, not a mini one.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How do I connect my Android phone to a mini projector wirelessly?
 Most Android phones connect via Miracast: swipe down to Quick Settings, tap Cast or Screen Mirroring, and select your projector. For Samsung phones, the option is called Smart View. The projector and phone must be on the same Wi-Fi network for this to work, unless your projector supports P2P direct connection (like the AKIYO O1).
 Can you connect an iPhone to a mini projector?
 Yes. iPhones connect to mini projectors via AirPlay for wireless mirroring, or via a Lightning to HDMI adapter for wired connection. Most projectors in this roundup support AirPlay out of the box – just enable Screen Mirroring in Control Center and select the projector.
 Can I use a mini projector with my iPhone without an adapter?
 Yes, if the projector supports AirPlay. Every wireless projector in this roundup (YGSKK, WEMI X7, Wielio, Magcubic, AKIYO, etc.) supports iPhone mirroring without any adapter. For HDCP-protected content like Netflix, you’ll still need a workaround like a Fire TV Stick.
 Can I project my phone to the wall?
 Yes, any mini projector in this roundup will project your phone screen onto a wall, ceiling, or projector screen. A flat, light-colored wall works fine for casual use. For the sharpest image, a dedicated projector screen is recommended but not required.
 Why can’t I mirror Netflix to my mini projector?
 Netflix uses HDCP (High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection) to prevent wireless mirroring. Most mini projectors can’t bypass this restriction. Three workarounds: use a Fire TV Stick or Roku plugged into the projector, buy a projector with officially licensed Netflix built-in (like the WEMI X7), or use a Lightning/USB-C to HDMI wired adapter.
 What is the best mini projector for iPhone?
 The YGSKK Mini Projector is our top pick for iPhone users: native 1080P, Wi-Fi 6, AirPlay support, 3-year warranty, and reliable wireless mirroring for under $80. For premium pick, the WEMI X7 with 2000 ANSI lumens and built-in Netflix runs around $189.
 Are mini projectors good for outdoor movies?
 Yes, but only after sunset or in deep shade. Most mini projectors need 300+ ANSI lumens for usable outdoor images at dusk. For daylight viewing, only the WEMI X7 (2000 ANSI) works. For post-sunset backyard movies, the YGSKK and Wielio 2026 are excellent mid-priced options.
 What is the difference between 1080p supported and native 1080p?
 1080p supported means the projector accepts a 1080p signal but displays it at a lower resolution (usually 720p). Native 1080p means the projector has 1920×1080 pixels and displays full HD content without downscaling. Native 1080p produces sharper text and detail, especially at 80+ inch image sizes.
 Final Verdict: Which Mini Projector Should You Buy?
 The best mini projectors for phones in 2026 come down to your budget and use case. If you want one projector that does everything – works in daylight, runs Netflix natively, and handles outdoor movie nights – the WEMI X7 is the clear winner. For most buyers, the YGSKK Mini Projector delivers the best balance of native 1080P, Wi-Fi 6, and value under $80. And if you’re shopping on a strict $40 budget, the CiBest W13 with its 10,000+ reviews won’t disappoint for dark-room use.

 You’re camping, and someone pulls out their phone to show a video. Everyone squints at the tiny screen. A mini projector could have turned that into an impromptu movie night. But which one actually works with your phone without a tangle of adapters? That’s the question we set out to answer. A true mini projector for phone use has to pair easily, throw a bright enough image to hold its own outdoors, and stay light enough to toss in a bag.
 Not all mini projectors are created equal. Some require a specific HDMI adapter for your iPhone or Android, while others connect wirelessly with a tap. Brightness varies wildly-from dim models that need total darkness to units that hold up under ambient light. We compared eight of the most interesting options across seven brands, focusing on what makes a projector genuinely phone-friendly. Whether you want a plug-and-play portable theater or a super-bright smart hub that cuts cords entirely, this guide has you covered.

 The H1 is the sharpest wired option and a solid choice if you already have the adapter and want true 1080p without paying for smart features.

 The TMY V08 bundles everything you need to get started, including an 80-inch foldable projection screen. It supports 1080p input, offers Bluetooth speaker connectivity plus a standalone speaker mode, and works with phones via a standard HDMI adapter-all at a very wallet-friendly price.

 For a complete out-of-the-box starter kit with screen and Bluetooth convenience, the TMY V08 is a practical wired pick at an unbeatable entry price.

 The CiBest W13 strips out all the extras to hit an ultra-budget price. There’s no WiFi, no Bluetooth, and no built-in apps-just a barebones HDMI projector that works with your phone if you supply the adapter. It’s tiny, simple, and backed by a massive number of positive reviews.

 The Good to Know:
 Zero wireless connectivity-you must use a cable. No keystone correction, so placement is finicky. Native resolution is 720p, and it cannot stream Netflix directly due to HDCP; you need a streaming stick or laptop. Sound is basic at best.
 Bottom Line:
 If budget is your only priority and you don’t mind wires, the CiBest W13 is a proven cheap way to project your phone’s screen in the dark.
 How We Evaluated These Mini Projectors for Phone
 We didn’t run these through a full season of field use. What we did: cross-referenced 8 mini projector models from 7 distinct brands across 7 decision axes -brightness, wireless connectivity, ease of phone mirroring, portability, resolution, built-in smart features, and value. We triangulated published specifications, aggregated owner feedback where available, and use-case fit against what phone users actually need in a portable projector. The scoring framework weighted real-world phone-compatibility (70%) -how well each model handles actual phone mirroring, adapter requirements, and streaming-against feature differentiation (30%) -unique specs like autofocus, Dolby Audio, dustproofing, and smart OS. We have no commercial relationship with any of the brands featured; recommendations track fit and differentiation, not brand preference. If you want the most polished wireless phone experience, the VOPLLS K3 is your match; if you value sheer brightness per dollar, the HAPPRUN H11 serves you better.
 How to Choose the Right Mini Projector for Phone
 1. What Makes a Projector 'Mini'?
 Mini doesn’t have a strict definition, but in this category we’re talking projectors under 5 pounds and small enough to fit in a daypack. The tiniest here, the WEMI X1BQ, weighs just 0.8 pounds and is no bigger than a soda can. Even the heaviest, the HAPPRUN H1 at 4.5 pounds, is still far easier to move than a full-size model. True mini projectors also trade some brightness for portability-don’t expect 3000-lumen performance, but the best ones compensate with efficient LEDs and good optics.
 2. How to Connect Your Phone to a Mini Projector
 This is the make-or-break spec for phone users. Projectors fall into two camps: wired and wireless. Wired models, like the HAPPRUN H1 and TMY V08 , require an HDMI adapter specific to your phone-Lightning to HDMI for iPhones, USB-C to HDMI for many Androids. That’s an extra purchase and one more cable to manage. Wireless projectors, like the YGSKK and VOPLLS K3 , either mirror your screen directly via AirPlay/Miracast or cast from within apps. The smoothest options use WiFi 6 and dedicated mirroring protocols, cutting the cord entirely.
 3. Wireless vs. Wired: Which Phone Connection Is Right for You?
 Wireless wins for convenience-tap a button and your phone’s screen appears. However, it can introduce slight lag that’s fine for video but noticeable in gaming. Wired connections are lag-free and more reliable, but you’ll need to buy the right adapter and keep your phone tethered. If you frequently stream DRM-protected content like Netflix, note that many projectors can’t mirror these apps due to copyright; the workaround is to use a streaming stick or choose a projector with built-in certified apps (like the VOPLLS K3 or HAPPRUN H11). Those models let you launch Netflix directly on the projector, bypassing the phone entirely.
 4. Brightness and Image Quality for Phone Projection
 Phone screens are small, so projection demands a bright, sharp image. ANSI lumens give a real-world brightness figure. For a truly dark room, 200-300 ANSI lumens works; for any ambient light, aim for 1000+ ANSI. The HAPPRUN H11 and VOPLLS K3 push 1500 ANSI, making them the best picks for less-than-pitch-black spaces. Resolution matters too-native 1080p (found on the XuanPad and HAPPRUN H1) reveals text and fine detail that 720p models soften. However, most phone content is 1080p or lower, so a sharp 720p with good optics can still satisfy.
 5. Built-in Smart Features vs. Basic Models
 Many mini projectors now ship with their own operating system and preloaded apps. This turns the projector into a standalone streaming hub.
